title: Luster Star-Shaped Tile
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
period: Seljuk / pre-Mongol [cataloguer, from the dated inscription. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Stonepaste; luster-painted on opaque glaze with inglaze painting
geometry: 8-pointed star formed by two overlapping squares, with an inner star-shaped field set inside a band of script
symmetry: Outline has 8-fold rotational symmetry with 8 mirror lines (D8). The figural field is not symmetric
imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, H.O. Havemeyer Collection, Gift of Horace Havemeyer, 1940. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Luster_Star-Shaped_Tile_MET_sf40-181-1a.jpg), licence CC0
notes: Observed: a large star (the API gives 32.1 cm diameter) with a court scene of a central seated figure flanked by attendants, all on a lustre ground scratched with small reserved spirals. A white border carries a cursive inscription in lustre. Turquoise inglaze dabs. Surface heavily worn and cracked. Interpretation: the standard Kashan lustre star format (figural field plus inscription border), useful as a template for the lustre star cell and its border band.
uncertainty: Met gives place as 'Attributed to Kashan'. Inscription not read or verified here.

title: Tile, Half Star
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
period: Seljuk / pre-Mongol [cataloguer, from the dated inscription. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Stonepaste; luster-painted on opaque white glaze under transparent colorless glaze
geometry: Half of an 8-pointed star, cut along a line through two opposite inner corners. Used to finish a star-and-cross field at a straight edge
symmetry: Outline has one mirror line (vertical). Figures are near-mirrored but not exact
imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1966. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tile,_Half_Star_MET_sf66-95-5.jpg), licence CC0
notes: Observed: half-star shape with a cobalt outline, a white band of lustre script around a figural field of two haloed figures in patterned robes over a scrolled lustre ground. Interpretation: evidence that star tilings were terminated with half tiles, relevant to edge handling in a girih/star panel generator.
uncertainty: Exact role of half stars within the original wall is not stated in the API record.

title: Star-Shaped Tile
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
period: Ilkhanid [cataloguer, from the date. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Stonepaste; luster-painted on opaque white glaze
geometry: 8-pointed star, inner star field with large reserved spiral scrolls whose edges are scalloped (split-leaf), plus small roundels
symmetry: Outline D8. Ornament is loosely rotational but not strictly symmetric
imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Edward C. Moore Collection, Bequest of Edward C. Moore, 1891. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Star-Shaped_Tile_MET_DP242536.jpg), licence CC0
notes: Observed: no figures. The field is a free spiral arabesque reserved in white against a lustre ground with tiny reserved spirals and dots. Inscription in lustre on the white border. Interpretation: a clean reference for a lustre eslimi fill inside a star cell.
uncertainty: Met record: 'Attributed to Kashan'. Dated 661 AH/1262–63 CE per the API.

title: Eight-pointed Star Tile Depicting Animals and Inscription
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
period: Ilkhanid [cataloguer, from the date. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Stonepaste; luster-painted on opaque white glaze under transparent glaze
geometry: 8-pointed star. A cobalt line scroll forms a four-lobed ogival armature that meets at the centre, with animals in the compartments
symmetry: Cobalt armature approximately D4 (4 mirror lines). Animals break the symmetry
imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, H.O. Havemeyer Collection, Gift of Horace Havemeyer, 1941. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Eight-pointed_Star_Tile_Depicting_Animals_and_Inscription_MET_DP257292.jpg), licence CC0
notes: Observed: cobalt strapwork ogees with split-palmette terminals divide the star into four compartments containing reserved animals on a dotted lustre ground. White border with lustre script, blue rim. Interpretation: shows how a 4-fold armature can be overlaid on an 8-fold star outline.
uncertainty: Met record: 'Attributed to Kashan', dated 665 AH/1267 CE.

title: Eight-pointed Star Tile with Foliage and Inscription
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
period: Ilkhanid [cataloguer, from the date. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Stonepaste; luster-painted on opaque white glaze under transparent glaze
geometry: 8-pointed star with a single asymmetric plant spray filling the inner star
imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, H.O. Havemeyer Collection, Gift of Horace Havemeyer, 1941. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Eight-pointed_Star_Tile_with_Foliage_and_Inscription_MET_DP247853.jpg), licence CC0
notes: Observed: a tree-like spray of reserved leaves and blossoms with turquoise dots and a cobalt flower near the top. The border text appears to begin with an Arabic phrase that reads like the opening of Qur'an 97 (al-Qadr). Interpretation: a free floral (khatai-like) fill within a lustre star.
uncertainty: The Qur'anic reading of the border is my own visual reading, not stated in the API record. Met: 'Made in probably Kashan'.

title: Panel Composed with Tiles in Shape of Eight-pointed Stars and Crosses
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
period: Ilkhanid [cataloguer, from the date 1260–70. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Stonepaste; luster-painted on opaque white glaze under transparent glaze
geometry: Classic star-and-cross tessellation: regular 8-pointed stars (two overlapping squares) alternating with four-armed cross tiles whose arm ends are pointed. The crosses fill exactly the gaps between stars
symmetry: Tiling outline is p4m (4-fold centres at star centres and cross centres, mirror lines along rows and diagonals). Individual tile fills differ, so the decorated panel has no strict symmetry
imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, H.O. Havemeyer Collection, Gift of Horace Havemeyer, 1941. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Panel_Composed_with_Tiles_in_Shape_of_Eight-pointed_Stars_and_Crosses_MET_DP251471.jpg), licence CC0
notes: Observed: about 17 stars and the crosses between them reassembled into a panel. Each star has its own fill (palmette medallions, birds, floral rosettes, a large teardrop medallion) with a white script border. The crosses are mostly speckled lustre with sparse reserved designs. Interpretation: the single best reference here for the star-and-cross layout and tile proportions, and a reminder that historic panels varied the fill per tile.
uncertainty: Met: 'Made in probably Kashan'. Whether this grouping reflects an original wall arrangement is not stated in the API record.

title: Cross-Shaped Tile
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
period: Seljuk or Ilkhanid [cataloguer, 13th-century date is not specific enough. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Stonepaste; luster-painted on opaque white glaze under transparent glaze
geometry: Cross tile with pointed (chamfered) arm ends, the companion shape to the 8-pointed star
symmetry: Outline D4. Fill has one approximate vertical mirror line
imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, H.O. Havemeyer Collection, Gift of Horace Havemeyer, 1941. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cross-Shaped_Tile_MET_41.165.34.jpg), licence CC0
notes: Observed: the available image is black and white, so no colours are recorded. A tree or plant rises from a base at the bottom arm, with a small fish shape below. Leaves are reserved on a dark ground. Interpretation: shows how a cross tile can carry a single upright plant rather than a centred motif.
uncertainty: Image is a black-and-white archival photograph, colour not observable. Met: 'Made in probably Kashan'.

title: Cross-Shaped Tile
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
period: Seljuk or Ilkhanid [cataloguer, 13th-century date is not specific enough. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Stonepaste; inglaze painted in blue and turquoise and luster-painted on opaque white glaze
elements: split-palmette ogival motifs on each arm
geometry: Cross tile with pointed arms and a raised rim, set among star tiles. Central disc with one ogival palmette unit per arm
imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, H.O. Havemeyer Collection, Gift of Horace Havemeyer, 1941. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cross-Shaped_Tile_MET_wb-41.165.37.jpeg), licence CC0
notes: Observed: photographed in situ among star tiles, so the joint between star points and cross arms is visible. Each arm holds a reserved ogival palmette with a fan of fine lines. Turquoise pools along the edges. Interpretation: a good model for a symmetric cross fill and for the moulded rim that separates tiles.
uncertainty: Met: 'Made in probably Kashan', 13th century.

title: Star-Shaped Tile
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
period: Seljuk or Ilkhanid [cataloguer, 13th-century date is not specific enough. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Stonepaste; inglaze painted in blue and turquoise and luster-painted on opaque white glaze

title: Hexagonal Tile
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
period: Seljuk or Ilkhanid [cataloguer, 13th-century date is not specific enough. Met API period field is empty]

geometry: Regular hexagon with an inner hexagonal frame line
imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Rafael Guastavino, 1928. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hexagonal_Tile_MET_sf28-89-8.jpg), licence CC0

uncertainty: Image downloaded at 500 px, the largest thumbnail available. Animal species not identified.

title: Pair of Tiles with Qur'anic Inscription from Sura 36 (Ya-Sin): 9 and 15
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
period: Seljuk or Ilkhanid [cataloguer, 13th-century date is not specific enough. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Stonepaste; molded and luster-painted on opaque white glaze under transparent glaze
elements: lustre ground with reserved arabesque scrolls
geometry: Rectangular frieze tile, letters raised in relief, ground filled with fine scrolls
imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, H.O. Havemeyer Collection, Gift of Horace Havemeyer, 1940. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pair_of_Tiles_with_Qur%27anic_Inscription_from_Sura_36_(Ya-Sin)-_9_and_15_MET_DP251469.jpg), licence CC0
notes: Observed: the downloaded image shows one rectangular tile of the pair. Tall letters glazed cobalt stand in relief above a reddish lustre ground of reserved scrolls. Interpretation: the two-layer frieze (relief script over a lustre arabesque ground) that defines Kashan inscription bands.
uncertainty: API title says 'Pair of Tiles with Qur'anic Inscription from Sura 36 (Ya-Sin)'. The image shows a single tile.

title: Tile Panel
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
period: Seljuk or Ilkhanid [cataloguer, 13th-century date is not specific enough. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Stonepaste; molded and luster-painted
elements: upper band of moulded split palmettes
geometry: Row of square tiles, each with a narrow upper arabesque band and a main field of large relief script
symmetry: Upper band is a translational frieze of repeated palmette units. Main band has no symmetry (text)

title: Tile Panel in the form of an Architectural Niche

period: Ilkhanid [cataloguer, from 'first half 14th century'. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Stonepaste; inglaze painted in blue, luster-painted on opaque white glaze, modeled
elements: relief inscriptions in field and borders
geometry: Tall rectangle of three tiles. Niche outline with a lobed arch on two colonnettes, framed by inscription bands on three sides
symmetry: Bilateral mirror symmetry of the niche architecture. Text breaks it
imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1909. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tile_Panel_in_the_form_of_an_Architectural_Niche_MET_DT11973.jpg), licence CC0

title: Tile with Niche Design

title: Tile from a Mihrab
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
period: Ilkhanid [cataloguer, from the date 722 AH/1322–23 CE. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Stonepaste; modeled, painted under transparent glaze
geometry: Pentagon (rectangle with a gable top). Two interlocking ogee loops form the central armature with palmette and blossom fills, framed by a text band

title: Tile from a Frieze

technique: Stonepaste; overglaze painted (so-called mina'i)
geometry: Square, two moulded arched bays between registers. Upper border is a row of hexagram stars in a band
symmetry: Approximate bilateral symmetry of the arcade. Borders are translational friezes
imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1911. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tile_from_a_Frieze_MET_wb-11.74.1.jpeg), licence CC0

uncertainty: API: 'Attributed to Iran', medium 'overglaze painted (so-called mina'i)'. The 'so-called' hedge is the Met's.

title: Tile with Image of Phoenix

title: Star- and Hexagonal-Tile Panel

geometry: Tiling of six-pointed stars (hexagrams) and regular hexagons. Each hexagon shares edges with star points

imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1937. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Star-_and_Hexagonal-Tile_Panel_MET_wb-37.40.26.jpeg), licence CC0

title: Tile Panel
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
period: Ilkhanid [cataloguer, from 'late 13th–first half 14th century'. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Mosaic of polychrome-glazed cut tiles on stonepaste body; set into mortar
geometry: Pieces include 5-pointed stars and irregular pentagons, typical of 5-fold or 10-fold geometric mosaic. The set appears in a modern circular mortar bed
symmetry: Local 5-fold elements. Overall arrangement not reliable (see uncertainty)

uncertainty: API title 'Tile Panel', geography 'Attributed to Iran'. The circular mounting looks like a storage or modern reassembly, so the layout may not be original.

title: Mihrab (Prayer Niche)
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
period: Mid 14th century, post-Ilkhanid [cataloguer, from the date 755 AH/1354–55 CE. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Mosaic of polychrome-glazed cut tiles on stonepaste body; set into mortar
elements: geometric strapwork with star and hexagon medallions in hood
geometry: Rectangular frame around a pointed arch. Tympanum filled with curvilinear strapwork. Hood carries a strapwork net of hexagonal and star compartments. Lower niche walls carry a repeating star lattice
symmetry: Bilateral overall. Lower lattice is a periodic geometric pattern, likely 4-fold based
imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1939. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Mihrab_(Prayer_Niche)_MET_DP235035.jpg), licence CC0

uncertainty: API geography: 'From Isfahan'. Medium: mosaic of polychrome-glazed cut tiles on stonepaste body, set into mortar. Accession 39.20 and the date are confirmed by the API.

title: Tile from a Squinch

title: Tile Decorated with Entrelacs Pattern Based on Octagons
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
origin: Made in Bukhara or Samarqand, present-day Uzbekistan
period: Probably early Timurid [cataloguer, from 'second half 14th century'. Met API period field is empty]
technique: Stonepaste; carved and glazed in turquoise and aubergine
geometry: Interlace (entrelacs) built on octagons: 8-pointed star centres surrounded by bands that weave over and under
symmetry: Each star centre is close to 8-fold. As a strip it is a frieze pattern with vertical and horizontal mirror lines (approximately p2mm frieze group)
imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Purchase, Walter D. Binger Gift, 1972. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tile_Decorated_with_Entrelacs_Pattern_Based_on_Octagons_MET_sf1972-88b.jpg), licence CC0
notes: Observed: carved relief, two band colours (pale turquoise and aubergine) interweaving. Interpretation: direct model for an 8-fold girih border with over-under weave.
uncertainty: API: 'Made in Bukhara or Samarqand', present-day Uzbekistan. Medium: carved and glazed in turquoise and aubergine.

Ettinghausen Gifts, in memory of Richard Ettinghausen; and Steven Kossak, Mrs. Charles Wrightsman, and Richard S. Perkins Gifts, 1995. uncertainty: API: 'Attributed to Iran', 'painted in black on a white ground under green glaze with traces of overglaze gold', colours not visible in the image. 3-fold reading is my own and uncertain.

title: Tile Panel
institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

technique: Stonepaste; polychrome glazed within black wax resist outlines (cuerda seca technique)
elements: eslimi border with split-palmette cartouches and rosettes
geometry: Rectangular pictorial field built of square tiles, framed by a continuous border of linked arabesque cartouches
symmetry: Field none. Border is a translational repeat with mirror symmetry in each unit
imageCredit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1903. Image file obtained via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tile_Panel_MET_DP152806.jpg), licence CC0
notes: Observed: a garden scene painted in cuerda seca colours with dark outlines, blue sky, white hills, green ground. Border of yellow-outlined palmette cartouches on cobalt. Interpretation: the key haft-rang figurative panel, and a model border.
uncertainty: API: 'Attributed to probably Isfahan'. Medium: polychrome glazed within black wax resist outlines (cuerda seca technique).

title: Luster Wall Tile with a Couple
institution: The Cleveland Museum of Art
period: Ilkhanid period (1256-1353) (as given by Cleveland)
technique: fritware with luster-painted design
geometry: 8-pointed star with inner star field and script border
symmetry: Outline D8. Composition near-bilateral about the central tree
imageRights: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
imageCredit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust by exchange
notes: Observed: a couple either side of a turquoise tree, birds in the corners, dense spiral ground. Source states the border carries Persian love poetry (two quatrains, transliterated and translated by the museum) and that the tile would have alternated with cross-shaped tiles. Interpretation: the clearest documented case here of Persian poetry on a lustre star.
uncertainty: Cleveland gives date 1266, place Kashan. Inscription text and translation are from the museum record.

notes: Observed: white moulded lotus and leaves outlined dark on a speckled cobalt ground. The museum notes star tiles were combined with cross-shaped tiles to cover walls. Interpretation: an underglaze (non-lustre) star, informs a two-colour khatai star cell.
uncertainty: Cleveland: 'probably Sultanabad', c. 1300–50.

title: Prayer Niche (Mihrab)
institution: The Cleveland Museum of Art
origin: Iran, Isfahan, in the style of the Safavid period (1501–1722)
period: In the style of the Safavid period (1501–1722) (as given by Cleveland)
technique: ceramic mosaic
elements: white thuluth inscription bands on cobalt
geometric star lattice on lower niche
geometry: Rectangular frame with inscription border, pointed arch niche, hood with lobed medallions, lower walls with a star lattice
imageRights: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
imageCredit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Katharine Holden Thayer
notes: Observed: complete cut-tile mosaic mihrab. The museum record states the Qur'anic text is from Surah an-Nur (the Light verse) in thuluth, white glaze with an arabesque vine in gold, turquoise and green. Interpretation: useful as a visual composition guide, but not as evidence of 16th-century practice.
uncertainty: Cleveland dates it 'c. 1500s or mid-1900s'. The record says thermoluminescence tests in 2001 indicated the tiles were made between 1941 and 1961 and are under further examination. Treat as a probable modern work in Safavid style.

title: Jameh Mosque of Isfahan (Masjed-e Jameh)
institution: Jameh Mosque of Isfahan (Masjed-e Jameh)
period: Multiple periods (Buyid, Seljuk, Ilkhanid, Aq Qoyunlu, Safavid, per source)
date: Seljuk dome chambers 1086–87 and 1088–89, tilework added later (per source)
technique: patterned brickwork, carved stucco, muqarnas, tilework (per source)
elements: brick patterns in circles, diamonds and zigzags
rich variety of geometric vault decoration
geometry: Brick geometric patterns and about 200 small vaults with different geometric designs (per source). Photo shows tiled iwan with muqarnas hood
imageCredit: seier+seier, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Friday_mosque_isfahan.jpg
notes: Source statements: Wikipedia (last resort): Buyid additions 'decorated with patterns created with bricks laid in circles, diamond shapes, zigzags, and other geometric patterns'. Smaller vaults 'display a rich variety of geometric decoration'. Southern iwan tilework 'originally added under the patronage of the Aq Qoyunlu ruler Uzun Hasan in 1475–6'. Safavid 'new tile revetment were added to the iwans and minarets'. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2012. Photo observed: view through the north iwan to the southern iwan with tiled facade, muqarnas hood and tiled minarets. Brick ornament with small tiled geometric inlays is visible on the foreground vault.
uncertainty: Reference is Wikipedia, used as a last resort and flagged. UNESCO page (whc.unesco.org/en/list/1397) blocked automated access, so Wikipedia is used. The Flickr photo caption also says the iwans are Seljuk with Safavid tile cladding, which is the photographer's statement.
